root.meaning: the Sabbath, the day of rest
root.note: Through Greek sábbaton and its variant sámbaton.

history: Samedi is two words in one: the Sabbath, and dies, Latin for ‘day’. The Sabbath is the Jewish day of rest, Hebrew shabbat, Greek sábbaton. Greek also had a form with an m, sámbaton, and from it Vulgar Latin made sambati dies, ‘the day of the Sabbath’. According to the TLFi, this Christian name pushed out the pagan one, dies Saturni, ‘Saturn's day’, in the 4th century, just as dies dominicus, ‘the Lord's day’, replaced dies solis, ‘the Sun's day’. That second one became dimanche. English kept both pagan names: Saturday and Sunday. The first French text with samedi is the Voyage of Saint Brendan, early in the 12th century. In French the days take no capital letter: à samedi !
historyEinfach: Samedi comes from Latin sambati dies: ‘the day of the Sabbath’. The Sabbath is the Jewish day of rest. Before, the Romans called this day ‘Saturn's day’. English still says Saturday. The Christians changed the name, and French kept the Christian one. Days have no capital letter in French: samedi, dimanche.

elsewhere.text: English kept the Roman god Saturn in the name of the day. French replaced him with the Sabbath, so the two names are not related.
